If a collection consists of two names and so forth, it is termed a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) and the like;
when there are three or more, it is further termed "many.
That which is called an "aggregate" (*skandha*) has the meaning of a "heap" or "accumulation."
That is to say, the eleven types of form, the five feelings, the six perceptions, the seventy-three formations, and the eight consciousnesses are each briefly condensed into a single aggregate;
thus they are named the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
The old translations of the sūtras and śāstras render this as "aggregate" (skandha);
this is because the term "aggregate," being brief, encompasses many meanings.
That which is called a "base" (āyatana) has the meaning of "source of arising" and the meaning of "gate."
This is because the six internal sense faculties and the six external objects are the bases where the six consciousnesses arise and grow;
these six faculties and objects are able to respectively facilitate the entry and exit of the six consciousnesses.
The old translation renders this as "entry" (入),
which loses the meaning of "arising" (生).
What is called a "realm" (界) has the sense of a "lineage" or "seed-stock" (種族).
This means that the six sense faculties, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses constitute the categories of faculty, object, and consciousness;
just as there are distinctions among the four castes and lineages,
the meaning of "lineage" (gotra) is thus termed the meaning of "element" (dhātu).
Therefore, the Abhidharmakośakārikā states:
"Aggregation, the gateway for arising, and lineage— these are the meanings of the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu)."
In the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, the meaning of the limits differs slightly from this;
I cannot describe it in detail here.
Those who find it interesting may recount it.
These are all the meanings that are expressed.
As for the phrase "appearing as external forms while in reality being only [consciousness]," it is like the flowers in the sky seen by one with cataracts in their eyes.
It appears to be outside the eye,
yet it actually resides within the eye.
Now, to reveal that internal phenomena appear as such through deluded perception:
This clarifies the refutation of external objections regarding the appearance of objects.
Specifically, an external objection states:
"If there were external phenomena that were the objects of resemblance, then external phenomena must exist."
If external phenomena do not exist, what would there be for it to resemble?
Since there is nothing to resemble, the sense of "resemblance" is not established.
How, then, can it be said that the mind resembles external objects?
Therefore, the present commentary explains:
that which is called "resemblance" (sādṛśya) refers to the manifestation of internal phenomena as resembling the grasping mind.
Regarding what is called "internal phenomena":
these are the objective aspects (nimittabhāga) manifested by the mind, which in reality exist only internally;
yet, due to deluded ignorance, they are grasped as being external to the mind.
Therefore, it is said that internal phenomena resemble those false mental constructions;
it is not said that internal phenomena resemble external objects.
As for the towering sea-palaces and the illusory structures of vapors [mirages], and so forth:
It is said that within the ocean there is an insect called a *śiṅku*,
shaped like a bee or a clam;
it comes to play upon the surface of the water, exhaling mist as its sport.
When the morning sun first shines, its vapor takes on the form of a tower;
people seeing it from afar claim the tower truly exists,
yet it is merely a mirage of vapors and not an actual tower.
Regarding the phrase "How is it that one observes the same yet encounters the different?"—
*di* (覿) means to see;
it means to gaze upon.
*Kàn* (瞰) also means "to look at.
*Liàng* (諒) means "trustworthy" or "faithful.
*Fǒu* (否) means "evil" or "bad."
This conceals the goodness.
It means that while water is one,
the four views differ.
Faith can indeed arise from the mind;
it is entirely distinct from the mental grasping of good and evil.
Regarding the phrase "seeking and so forth during the stage of application":
In this context, the phrasing is inverted.
It should correctly be stated as:
"seeking that which exists conventionally but is non-existent in reality, [one forms] views."
This means that at the time when the wisdom of applied practice (*prayoga-jñāna*) is correctly arising,
all investigative comprehension and cognitive vision regarding [phenomena] as conventionally existent but ultimately non-existent is called "investigation" (*vitarka*).
Next, "sealing and grasping through receptivity" (*kṣānti*) refers to that which is without equal.
This means that there are three grades of patience (*kṣānti*).
When lower patience arises, one seals the non-existence of the grasped object while observing the grasper.
At the stage when middle patience evolves, one correctly observes the grasper itself.
Just as that which is grasped is definitely non-existent, so too,
at the stage where the higher patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) arises, one definitively seals that the graspable is empty.
In this present passage, the text concerning the higher patience is omitted.
The following passage is exactly as it appears in the text below.
Now, to reaffirm that this is definitively non-existent,
it constitutes the stage of "lower patience" (mṛdu-kṣānti).
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "the mind that can grasp, having confronted the object" refers to medium-level patience (*madhyamā kṣānti*).
Although this patience likewise confirms the subject that grasps and so forth, [it does not yet realize their ultimate non-existence].
This is precisely the "superior patience" (adhimātra-kṣānti).
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the essence of the object extends to both the internal and external," a question is asked:
Regarding how these internal and external objects relate to the two types of conditions— the direct and the indirect—
among the four conditions,
the seventh chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* extensively elucidates their characteristics.
Now, to briefly enumerate them:
first is the condition as cause (*hetu-pratyaya*),
which refers to conditioned phenomena directly producing their own effects.
This essence has two aspects:
seeds and active manifestations. Regarding seeds:
This refers to the functional distinctions within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) among the various realms (dhātu), stages (bhūmi), and types (gati)— whether wholesome,
defiled, or indeterminate— which are capable of inducing subsequent functions of their own kind and giving rise to simultaneous manifest results of their own kind.
This refers solely to the fact that, in relation to those [seeds], they constitute the nature of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

"Manifesting" refers to the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) along with their associated mental factors, as well as the perceived objects (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving subjects (*darśana-bhāga*) they transform.
Excluding the wholesome states of the fruit of Buddhahood and the most inferior indeterminate states,
all others perfume the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) to produce seeds of their own kind;
these alone, in relation to those [subsequent states], constitute the nature of the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya).
The term "cause" (hetu) is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is itself the condition.
Second is the *samanantarapratyaya* (equal-and-immediate condition);
it was also formerly called the *anantarapratyaya* (sequential condition).
This refers to the eight manifest consciousnesses and their associated mental factors;
the preceding group, in relation to the subsequent group of its own kind,
provides equal guidance and leads them to arise with certainty.
Since the eight consciousnesses are not of the same category when compared with one another and arise simultaneously,
they do not serve as mutual equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Although mental factors and the mind always arise together, [they likewise do not function as such conditions].
Because they are associated despite not being of the same substantial nature,
they are blended as if into one;
it is impossible to designate them as separate or distinct.
Therefore, they can mutually serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Third is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
that is, if there is a phenomenon which the mind or its associated mental factors apprehend as their objective support by bearing its own characteristics.
This essence is of two kinds:
first, direct; second, indirect.
If it is not separate from the essence of the cognitive faculty that apprehends it, [it is direct].
That which is internally relied upon by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and so forth should be known as the direct objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*).
Even if it is spatially separated from the essence of the cognizing subject, [it remains the object].
That which serves as the substance capable of giving rise to what is internally contemplated and relied upon should be known as the remote objective condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*);
the immediate objective condition (*sākṣālambanapratyaya*), however, exists for all that is capable of cognition.
Because that which relies on an internal object of cognition does not arise in its absence;
whereas, as for the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
the subject that cognizes it may still arise even in the absence of an external object of cognition.
The fourth is the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
This refers to any phenomenon that possesses a superior power or efficacy capable of being either favorable or adverse toward other phenomena.
Although the first three conditions also possess predominance,
the fourth condition here excludes those and takes up the remainder in order to demonstrate the distinctions among the various conditions.
What is stated here regarding the pervasion of external objects does not refer to the "object of observation" (ālambana) mentioned in the third [section] of the Commentary.
This is because even that object of observation is not separate from consciousness.
It cannot be said that these are external objects existing outside the mind;
rather, it is only the "real" objects imagined by deluded sentiments and various false attachments that are designated as "external.
Therefore, one may say that they exist externally in terms of [deluded] perception, but internally in terms of [ultimate] reality.
If it exists externally even apart from its coarse object,
then external grasping would also be called true knowledge;
how, then, can it be said to be false grasping?
Answer: The apprehension of objects by the eye and other [senses] is merely direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
it cannot conceptually differentiate or insistently grasp them as being external.
Subsequently, as mental discrimination forcefully gives rise to external appearances,
they are said to be false because they do not correspond to reality;
one understands that they exist only nominally and lack substantial reality.
Observing the meaning of this master’s explanation,
it is intended to say that the thorough knowledge that things exist only nominally and lack substantial reality is the wisdom of investigation.
The definitive knowledge of practice obtained by means of this cause is called "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūtajñāna*).
When one examines the intent of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it differs from this [explanation].
The investigation into the view that things exist conventionally but lack intrinsic reality is called "seeking" (*vitarka*);
it is the thorough understanding of the view that things exist conventionally but lack intrinsic reality.

This is called "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). Therefore, knowing that [things] exist conventionally but lack substantial reality is not the wisdom of discursive investigation (*vitarka-jñāna*).
Since the original commentary is thus, [the conclusion follows].
Furthermore, regarding the practice of definitive resolution based upon [this],
it means that the knowledge of reality as it is constitutes the definitive practice and understanding that [phenomena] are conventionally existent but ultimately non-existent.
This refers to the destruction of the perception of subtle, pure characteristics in phenomena.
That is to say, if one is able to sever those phenomena characterized by defilement,
one can then realize those phenomena characterized by sublime purity;
these phenomena characterized by purity are precisely suchness (*tathatā*).
Because "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) has the meaning of "essential characteristic" (svabhāva-lakṣaṇa),
one who cannot sever defiled phenomena (saṃkleśa-dharma) fails to realize suchness (tathatā) because correct knowledge (samyag-jñāna) is destroyed.
Therefore, it is said that the characteristics of the dharma of verified purity are destroyed.
Regarding "the dharma of dwelling in indolence and the dharma of movement," this means that for one who is indolent,
there is both the dharma of that which is dwelt upon and the dharma of that which is moved.
It is firmly guarded and remains entirely without loss or destruction.
That which was previously described as the phenomenon characterized by affliction is called the "phenomenon in which [the mind] abides."
This is subject to destruction;
because it is unstable,
it is called a phenomenon of movement.
It is never separated from affliction;
therefore, those who are indolent are deeply pitiable.
Yet, they are still unable to eliminate the characteristics of emptiness and existence.
This means that in the three preceding stages, one contemplates the non-existence of the two grasps (grāhaka and grāhya), viewing them as conventionally existent but ultimately non-existent.

Therefore, at the stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma (laukikāgradharma), one simultaneously seals both types of emptiness and likewise attains the contemplative wisdom that perceives them as conventionally existent but ultimately non-existent.
That which exists conventionally is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva);
this is the aspect of existence.
That which is ultimately non-existent is the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).
This is called "signlessness.
When the ultimate truth is realized, both signs are extinguished;
therefore, the Worldly Supreme Dharma has not yet realized the ultimate truth.
Regarding the statement that "the Four Noble Truths and so forth" refers to "and so forth":
it means that those Four Noble Truths are established through sixteen modes of differentiation, which are called the "truths of formal establishment.
As for these sixteen modes:
These are the four aspects for each of the Four Noble Truths. Regarding the four aspects of the Truth of Suffering, they are:
impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
The four aspects of the truth of origination are:
cause, accumulation, arising, and condition. The four aspects of the truth of cessation are: [cessation, tranquility, excellence, and escape].
Cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation.
Regarding the four aspects of the Truth of the Path:
path, method, practice, and deliverance.
Having consulted both the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra*,
it is explained that they are clearly and easily understood as follows:
because they possess arising and ceasing, they are impermanent.
It is suffering because of its oppressive nature;
it is empty because it contradicts the view of "mine";
and it is non-self because it contradicts the view of "self."
It is a cause (*hetu*) because it is capable of producing phenomena;
it is accumulation (*samudaya*) because it is manifold;
it is arising (*jāti*) because it constantly nurtures and produces them.
It is a condition because it assists each [aggregate] individually;
it is cessation because all aggregates are exhausted;
it is peace because the three characteristics have subsided.
It is "sublime" because it is free from all afflictions;
it is "detached" because it is liberated from all calamities;
it is the "path" because its meaning is that of universal practice.
It is "truth" (*satya*) because it accords with correct principle;
it is "path" (*mārga*) because it correctly leads toward [the goal];
it is "exit" (*niḥsaraṇa*) because it enables one to transcend [suffering] forever.
Third, "the uninterrupted, the liberated, and the superior progress" refers to when one first gives rise to noble wisdom from preparatory application;
the afflictions that ought to be abandoned are severed entirely in a single moment of thought, with no intervening moments.
This is called the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*). It first severs the seeds of the hindrances and subsequently abandons the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*),
thereby realizing the wisdom of true suchness (*tathatā*) that is liberated from the afflictions previously severed.
It is called the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
It refers to all preparatory applications (*prayoga*) for the purpose of further severing remaining categories of afflictions and realizing further spiritual qualities.
The various paths of the superior categories of uninterrupted liberation are collectively termed "progressive advancement" (viśeṣa-mārga). Therefore,
the path of progressive advancement is likewise not separate from the preceding paths of uninterrupted liberation and liberation.
To progress from moment to moment is precisely what is called "superior advancement. Therefore,
the preceding [passage] spoke only of two [types of paths],
namely, the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Alternatively, regarding the general and the specific, one distinguishes the progressive advancement:
for instance, when severing the three upper grades of afflictions of the desire realm,
one must give rise to an uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and a path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for each respective grade.
In summary, this [path] initiates the superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) by abandoning the three middle grades;
therefore, this passage allows for three moments of mind.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* provides many other types of explanations regarding the meaning of the superior path through various successive methods.
Fearing prolixity, I shall not enumerate them all.
Regarding those who can eliminate the levels of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*), the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and so forth:
this refers to the fact that the wisdom of the path of seeing consists of three grades.
The lower grade of the path is termed "Heat" (*uṣmagata*),
because its power is weak when it first arises.
Since the conceptual afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*) to be abandoned by this path are already coarse and violent, [the lower grade is so named].
It is not called "Heat.
Therefore, the *Śrāvakabhūmi* states:
"Only the afflictions distinguished by one's own path of seeing [are abandoned]."
However, as for the "level of heat" (*ūṣmagata*),
it is called the "level of heat" because it is abandoned by the path of seeing; it refers to the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of the afflictions that are abandoned by the path of seeing.
If one follows the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*,
both the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the path (*mārga*) are each divided into nine grades,
namely: weak-weak and so forth.

That is to say, one abandons the superior and most superior delusions by means of the superior and most superior path, and abandons the moderate and most moderate delusions by means of the moderate and most moderate path; here,
for the sake of brevity, it is stated only in general terms.
Regarding the third pair, the simultaneous contemplation of the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena:
previously, due to inferior intellectual power, one contemplated and severed them individually;
now, because intellectual power is superior, one contemplates them simultaneously.
Question:
What further obstacles are there to the third contemplation? Answer:
This is the path of seeing through signs (*lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga*), not the true path of seeing (*bhūtadarśanamārga*).
Because it is a provisional designation based on a simulation of the truth, it is said that [afflictions] are abandoned;
thus, the initial wisdom is inferior, as it abandons [afflictions] through individual observation.
The third, the excellence of wisdom, is illustrated all at once. Regarding the second,
the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*),
the wording here is abbreviated.
If expressed fully, it should be called "the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*).

This is because it refers to the knowledge of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga-jñāna*) obtained immediately after the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering.
However, for the sake of brevity, it is simply called "the dharma-knowledge of suffering."
This is not the explanation.
What is the difference between this and the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*)?
Regarding that which is the predominant teaching arising from the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*):
This refers to the teachings concerning the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Because these teachings arise based upon the Truth of Suffering, they are called "teachings arising from the Truth of Suffering.
These teachings serve as the objective condition (*ālambana*) for the knowledge of suffering within the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga*) for all practitioners.
This teaching is called "superior" (adhipateya).
Regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering within the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga),
it refers to the knowledge of suffering that arises based upon the teachings.

Because it serves as the preparatory cause (*upāya-hetu*) for the receptivity to the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) is called the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
This is because it is capable of discerning the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) and so forth.
Question:
Since it is stated that this is realized through the path of vision involving conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*),
it is clearly understood that it is subsumed under the path of vision with images (*sanimitta-mārga*).
Why was it previously stated that these are established within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
The answer is:
in reality, both the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation possess both types of wisdom.
Each [system] distinguishes the principle realized by itself;
yet within those treatises,
they are explained according to the relative prominence or subtlety of the meanings concerning the benefit of oneself and others, appearing or remaining hidden accordingly.
This means that on the first stage (*bhūmi*), one is able to benefit oneself;
within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one first attains self-benefit.
True insight (*tattvadarśana*) increases while the function of conceptual perception (*nimittadarśana*) becomes subtle.
However, the hidden characteristics of true vision are not discussed here;
rather, regarding the benefit of others that arises during the path of cultivation,
the function of primordial wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is subtle while the function of subsequent wisdom (*prṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*) is predominant.
The fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the hidden [path] refers only to the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

Therefore, it is said that all right views (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) belonging to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) conceptually discern the principle realized by oneself on the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
In reality, however, this conceptual discernment pertains to the principle realized by one's own fundamental wisdom within the path of cultivation itself.
Regarding those who cultivate each of the perfections individually in this manner:
Question:
Do the ten stages (daśabhūmi) entirely lack the characteristics of the practice of the ten perfections?
How can it be falsely claimed that this constitutes the cultivation of the one? Answer:
Here, it is spoken of merely by way of analogy according to its meaning.
Why must their practices necessarily be identical?
It is said that the second stage receives the name "Stainless" (vimalā),
whereas the tenth stage achieves the Great Dharma-knowledge (mahādharma-jñāna).
From this it may be inferred that the various perfections (pāramitās) are cultivated separately in the other stages;
however, only one corner is cited because the remaining three corners follow by analogy.
Furthermore, it says:
Because the ten perfections vary in their coarseness and subtlety,
and their ease or difficulty, each preceding one induces the subsequent one;
since the preceding ones are coarse, they are easier to practice.
Because each subsequent stage is more subtle, it is difficult to cultivate;
thus, one should know that the ten perfections are practiced progressively and individually.
Furthermore, it is said:
True Suchness possesses two kinds of merit:
first, the ten aspects of True Suchness that are primordially present;
second, the ten kinds of superior practices that are newly produced.
Since the ten stages (bhūmi) of the true fundamental virtue are distinct as they are realized,
the practices newly generated at each stage are cultivated differently;
nevertheless, the names of the stages and their corresponding practices are identical.
Fearing that the meaning of the "mixed cultivation of the path" might be lost,
the names and characteristics of the stages and the practices are explained through the interplay of their similarities and differences, based on whether they are mixed or pure.
According to the facts, both obstacles obstruct both fruits:

because it is taught that the afflictive obstacle (kleśāvaraṇa), being deluded regarding the principles of the truths, obstructs the wisdom of self-emptiness (pudgala-śūnyatā) and thereby obstructs bodhi;
and because the cognitive obstacle (jñeyāvaraṇa), through its fear of the principle of dharma-emptiness, prevents it from manifesting and thereby obstructs nirvāṇa.
The afflictive obscurations [obstruct] nirvāṇa;
the cognitive obscurations [obstruct] bodhi.
This is stated in the subsequent text itself.
There is no need to cite this at length.
To speak of it specifically regarding the initial hindrance and so forth means that it is explained according to the distinct characteristics where those characteristics are predominant.
Because the afflictive hindrances can induce birth and death, they obstruct nirvāṇa;
because the cognitive hindrances obstruct the arising of wisdom, they obstruct bodhi.
As for the statement that their nature consists of defiled wisdom and so forth:
However, all five evil views take the wisdom of the "distinct objects" (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*) as their essential nature.
Since this wisdom of distinct objects pertains to all three moral natures,
it is here termed "defiled wisdom" because it is taken in its two [unwholesome and obscured-neutral] natures.
Defilement (rañjana) encompasses both the unwholesome (akuśala) and the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta).
Obscuration (nīvaraṇa) is itself defilement,
because it obstructs the noble path.
Therefore, both evil and concealment are termed "defiled.
Regarding the phrase "first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth":
this is because all secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and all primary afflictions (*kleśa*) are termed "grasping" (*upādāna*).
The aggregates arise from grasping, and are therefore called "aggregates of grasping" (*upādānaskandha*).
As the old commentary states, these are the "five burgeoning aggregates" (*pañca skandhāḥ saṃvartanīyāḥ*),
because the aggregates flourish intensely through the power of the afflictions.
The term "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānaskandha*) excludes the untainted aggregates (*anāsravaskandha*),
because it is only by depending on the tainted aggregates that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises.
Now, this view of a self-identity [arises] with respect to the body of the aggregates of clinging.
Some grasp two [aggregates] as the self,
some grasp one as the self,
and they grasp the remainder as "mine."
Because they involve indeterminate grasping, they are called "shifting views.
As for the phrase "the twenty-six [types of] views and so forth," these sixty-two are themselves false views.
This is explained in detail in works such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Abhidharmasamudaya*;
it shall be analyzed extensively in the *Śata-dharma-śāstra-vyākhyā*.
Furthermore, regarding the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and so forth that serve as the basis for vision:
The view that arises based on the aggregates is called the "basis of views.
Since one clings to these views as supreme and capable of purification,
and since this view is not separate from its basis— the five aggregates— [it follows that the self is not distinct from them].
Therefore, the aggregates that serve as its basis are likewise supreme purity.
The same applies to the clinging to precepts and observances;
there is no need to state it again at length.
"Those whose nature is stubborn and perverse":
"shang" (上) is pronounced with the *hu* and *ken* rhymes; it means to oppose or contravene.
Xià (pronounced with the "lì" and "jì" finals):
to bend. According to the *Shuowen*, it means to be deeply resentful and not accept admonition.
Regarding "one's own prosperity and so forth," this refers to one's noble lineage, physical beauty, abundant wealth, extensive learning, observance of precepts, disciples, retinue,
and even all other superior qualities pertaining to the body.
All these are called auspicious events.
"Not regarding one's own dharma" refers to the superior dharmas possessed by one's own person.
This refers precisely to those who possess a noble lineage, extensive learning, and so forth;
yet, although their bodies possess such superior qualities and they ought all the more to aspire toward the wholesome,
they disregard the excellent dharmas inherent within themselves.
One does not honor or respect virtuous and excellent persons.
Regarding those who cannot endure [faults] in those possessing actual virtue and capability:
"actual" refers to the reality and principle of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
"Virtue" refers to the true and pure virtues of the Three Jewels;
"capacity" refers to the superior functional power of all wholesome qualities.
Among these three types:
Because the mind cannot endure it and the will does not find pleasure in it,
it is called "lack of faith" (āśraddhya).
Regarding the eighth [root], which is exclusively non-obscured (anivṛta) and so forth:
However, there are generally two types of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*):
namely, the distinction between the obscured (*nivṛta*) and the unobscured (*anivṛta*).
If it is the unobscured type, it is not associated with afflictions (*kleśa*).
If there is an acquisition (*prāpti*) that arises simultaneously with an obscured defilement,
"obscured" refers to afflicted phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*),
because they obstruct the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
It is called "unobscured" because it does not obstruct the noble path;
the eighth [consciousness] is exclusively unobscured-neutral, unlike the manas.
Although these are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*),
because they are obscured (*nivṛta*) and associated with afflictions (*kleśa*), the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are not equal [to them].
Because it is necessary to weigh and compare degrees of superiority and inferiority before conceit,
over-conceit (*atimāna*), and so forth can arise;
for this reason, there are seven distinct types of conceit.
This is explained in detail in the *Vijñaptimātra-śata-dharma-śāstra-vyākhyā*.
Regarding the "great eight" within the seventh consciousness:
these eight types pervade all defiled minds and possess superior power.
It is therefore called "great.
Thus, the sixth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
"These twenty types are divided into three categories."
This means that because the ten afflictions beginning with anger (*krodha*) arise individually, they are called the minor secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Because the two beginning with lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) pervade all unwholesome states, they are called the intermediate secondary afflictions.
Because the eight beginning with restlessness (*auddhatya*) pervade all defiled minds, they are called the major secondary afflictions.

Regarding the statement, "However, there are generally two kinds of abandoning afflictions," this refers to the first of the four meanings of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), namely,
the path that is capable of effecting the transformation.
The "severing of the seeds" and so forth refers to the path of abandonment;
"and so forth" includes the state of unserviceability (*akarmanyatā*).
The two [types of abandonment] consist merely of suppression, which is the path of subduing.
This should be explained in detail according to the previous meaning.
Furthermore, regarding those who attain sudden enlightenment during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*),
there are generally two types of bodhisattvas.
The first is sudden enlightenment;
the second is gradual enlightenment.
This applies to those of indeterminate nature.
Furthermore, those who resolve their minds [for enlightenment] from the untainted noble stages of the two vehicles are called bodhisattvas of gradual awakening.
Consequently, there are five such types of persons:
namely, those of the four fruits and the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha.
They practice for a duration of eight, six, four, two, and one *kalpas* respectively.
Only then does one first attain the initial mind of the Ten Abodes.
Because the mind of the Two Vehicles obstructs the Mahāyāna,
it takes many kalpas before reaching the First Abode.
Therefore, a sutra states:
"The srotāpanna, through eighty thousand kalpas, contemplates the mind within its original state and realizes the emptiness of self.
Thus, during the stage of the provisions (sambhārāvasthā), there is the activity of untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna).
If those of the Mahāyāna lineage directly generate the great mind from the stage of an ordinary person,
this is called sudden enlightenment (*tongwu*).
However, because they practice the ten worldly paths of wholesome action for ten thousand kalpas, they attain entry into the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*).
Therefore, the stage of equipment (sambhāra-avasthā) consists solely of outflow-tainted (sāsrava) states,
as untainted (anāsrava) wisdom has not yet arisen in actual manifestation.
Alternatively, it may be understood as the opposite of this.
If it arises through reflection,
it is not suppressed at this stage.
If it arises due to a false teacher or false teachings, [it is likewise not suppressed].
This stage is capable of subduing [the afflictions].
Now, examining these two meanings, this principle is necessarily so;
for it is difficult to subdue the subtle [afflictions] that arise within the mind through one's own internal reflection.
Because they arise from external conditions such as heterodox teachings and heterodox teachers, they are easily abandoned.
Regarding the phrase "by practicing the three kinds of antidotes," there is a heading and an explanation for each of the three meanings.
This can be understood according to the text.

As for the subsequent statement regarding "the path preceded by right view that brings about permanent abandonment," it refers to the noble wisdom attained in the first stage (*bhūmi*), which is capable of permanently abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, it is called the right view of perpetual abandonment.
These three types constitute the path of preliminary application prior to the [main] path;
therefore, they are called the preliminary path.
Regarding the question of from what these abandonments are obtained:
the meaning of these various abandonments is somewhat difficult to grasp,
as I have not yet seen the original commentary.
Furthermore, let me offer one interpretation.
Should there be any other meaning, it shall be revised and corrected.
That is to say, the obstacles to be abandoned are of two kinds.
First is the latent predisposition (*dausthulya*),
and second is the active manifestation (*samudācāra*). From which of these are they severed?
However, the obstructions to be abandoned are not separate from the three periods of time. From which period are they abandoned?
The answer is: they are not abandoned from the past, and so forth.
The meaning intended here is that one does not abandon manifest afflictions;
for when the Path arises, the manifest afflictions have already ceased to exist.
That which has passed away in the past has already ceased and thus no delusion can be severed therein;
that which has not yet arrived in the future likewise cannot be severed;
and the present path does not coexist [with the afflictions], so there is nothing therein to be severed.
Therefore, it is not through the present delusions of the three periods of time that they are severed.

However, the phrase "from the heaviness (*dausthulya*) of the various afflictions" serves to resolve an objection and clarify the meaning of severance: if there were no delusions to be severed within the three periods of time, [how could severance occur]?
For what reason do the various teachings speak of the abandonment of afflictions? To this, he replies:
"Even though there is no sense of abandoning present afflictions," [it is so stated].
It may be designated as "severance" based on the seeds of heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Since "ran" (then/if) carries the sense of permission or concession,
the phrase "for the sake of severing such and such [afflictions]" is used.
At the time of the preparatory application, in order to permanently sever such coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*),
one gives rise to this antidote;
as the path of the remedy is correctly arising, the coarse heaviness is correctly ceasing.
Therefore, the designation "abandoned" is applied in reference to the *dausthulya* (coarse heaviness),
for there is no abandonment in reference to the active manifestations (*samudācāra*).
As for the phrase "because of the dissociation from this category," etc.:
This means that because the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of this category are extinguished,
future and present afflictions lack a cause and do not arise;
because they never arise again, it is called the "abandonment of afflictions."
This does not mean that the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) actually arise to sever the afflictions.
This intent does not speak of severing those [afflictions] of the three times;
rather, according to the original explanation, it does not speak of severing their "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) across the three times.
If that is so, why did the preceding text state:
"If the antidote for this category arises, then the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of this category is extinguished," and so forth?
For this reason, one can only say that the active afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three times are not severed.
Regarding the initial point concerning the gate of negation (*pratiṣedha*) and the non-interruption of the three periods of time and so forth:
both the *Saṃgrahābhidharmasamuccaya* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* contain the meanings of both "interruption" and "non-interruption.
The *Saṃgraha* specifically explains interruption and non-interruption in terms of both seeds (*bīja*) and active manifestations (*samudācāra*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of interruption and non-interruption in terms of the continuity of moments (*kṣaṇa*) according to their respective types;
each clarifies its meaning based on its own specific sense, so that they do not contradict one another.
Thus, regarding the meaning of non-interruption, the two texts are identical.
That which is associated with right view and capable of counteracting the mind refers to right view as the factor of right view within the Eightfold Noble Path;
that which is capable of counteracting the mind is precisely the wisdom of the fundamental reality (samyag-jñāna).
Because this right view is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and is able to discern what was realized on the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*),
it is associated with the mind that acts as its antidote. Thus,
this subsequently attained wisdom is associated with right view and is essentially untainted (*anāsrava*).
This is precisely what is called "the ability to treat the mind.
Regarding the phrase "in the present there are no latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and so forth," this indicates that there is no state of severance across all three periods of time.
Because all phenomena arise from a multitude of conditions in every moment and lack intrinsic nature;
because they perish necessarily in each instant and possess no functional activity;
and because they exist only momentarily in the present and are thus non-existent, their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) cease without depending on further abandonment.
How could this Noble Path be able to act as its antidote? Moreover,
since the obstacle and its remedy cannot coexist in a single moment, and darkness and light do not exist simultaneously,
how can there be any sense of "severance"?
Therefore, there are no latent dispositions (anuśaya) in the present world.
Since there are not even latent dispositions in the present world,
how much less could there be anything to be abandoned when one enters the past?
Even after this single thought-moment of the present,
as for the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that arise in the future and exist in the future world,
there are likewise none among them that are to be abandoned.
Therefore, within every moment of thought, this meaning of non-interruption applies.
From this point onward, regarding the phrase "in what has already been attained" and so forth,
the following section clarifies the meaning of that which is to be abandoned.
This means that although the aforementioned correct wisdom has no sense of severance within the present moment of mindfulness,
those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are nonetheless severed in every thought-moment.
This is because all phenomena possess a gateway of immovable continuity within mindfulness.
From the perspective of the gate of immobility, there is the meaning of non-interruption;
for all phenomena perish in each moment and thus lack the functional meaning of transition or movement.
From the perspective of the gate of continuity, there is the meaning of interruption.
Because the preceding thought-moment induces the arising of the succeeding thought-moment,
and because the causal conditions of this continuity perform a functional activity;
it is like a lamp, which, although it does not destroy darkness moment by moment, [continues to illuminate].
Just as darkness is dispelled by the continuity of flames,
so it is with all phenomena such as water, the moon, and the sun;
one should know that the principle here is likewise the same.
Therefore, by the power of the continuity of the noble path, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are simultaneously severed and the fundamental transformation (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) is attained.
For this reason, it is said that from this point onward, within the continuum of the body that has undergone transformation, and so forth.
Regarding "all subsequent worldly [minds] and so forth":
this means that because one has abandoned the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) through right knowledge,
one causes the subsequently attained uncontaminated noble wisdom (*anāsrava-āryajñāna*), as well as worldly wholesome and neutral minds, to arise.
Because there are no latent dispositions (anuśaya) binding it during all three times,
it is therefore called "completely free from latent dispositions.
The "indeterminate mind" (avyākṛta-citta) refers here to the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) mentioned in the text.

Answer: According to the explanation based on those three minds of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), these are precisely the preceding paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), liberation (*vimuktimārga*), and special progress (*viśeṣamārga*).
However, upon careful examination, this explanation is not logically correct.
Since the various afflictions of the three realms are abandoned all at once in a single moment during the path of seeing,
and since no distinction is made between their categories when they are abandoned,
multiple paths of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) do not arise separately.
What need is there for those words?
Because they state that "in order to sever such-and-such categories of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*),
one gives rise to such-and-such categories of antidotes," it is known that these repeated expressions do not refer to the three moments of mind within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
This is merely stated in conjunction with the path of cultivation that follows the path of seeing;
the Abhidharma clarifies the meaning of abandonment across all stages,
and does not speak of abandonment solely in reference to the initial path of seeing.
Between these two interpretations, the latter is stated to be correct.
Regarding the statement that "the lower grades of the two obstacles are collectively termed the third," a question is asked:
All treatises state that these three minds are established based on the general and specific aspects of the path of insight (*darśanamārga*).
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says:
"The first two are called dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*)."
Because it understands each [category] individually,
the third is called "subsequent knowledge" (anvaya-jñāna). Because it understands them collectively, it is so named.

However, this third [category] is established based on the general observation of the characteristics of abandonment regarding both the afflictive and cognitive obscurations (*kleśa-āvaraṇa* and *jñeya-āvaraṇa*).
How can these two obscurations be said to be of "inferior grade" (*mṛdu*)?
Furthermore, by what other obscuration would they be considered inferior?
Answer: That very unserviceability (akarmaṇyatā) of those two obstacles,
being a state of heaviness (dausthulya), is described as the inferior grade.
What logical fault is there in its being the third? If that were so,
one would also have to admit the existence of a middle grade.
Furthermore, by what dharma is the middle grade defined?
The answer is:
both the sūtras and the śāstras state that there are three types of *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness).
Because they are distinguished as being in the skin, in the flesh, and in the bone,
the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) likewise consist of three grades;
therefore, the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) has three grades of obstacles.
Regarding the statement "as the grasper and the truths of the higher and lower," the establishment of the sixteen [aspects] based on the contemplation of the two graspings is as follows:
the grasped object is precisely the suchness (*tathatā*) of the four truths.
The grasper is the wisdom that takes suchness as its object.
Based on the contemplation of the grasped, there are eight types of contemplative mind established as the patience and wisdom of the dharma;
based on the contemplation of the grasper, there are eight types of contemplative mind established as the patience and wisdom of subsequent realization.

This can be established by relying on the contemplation of the distinction between the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*), resulting in sixteen mental states (*citta*) categorized as dharmas and their classes.
All their respective modes of activity (*ākāra*) are self-evident from the text itself.
These sixteen [states] are based on the contemplation of the upper and lower [realms].
"Upper" refers to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); "lower" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Based on the contemplation of the suchness (*tathatā*) of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) within the desire realm, the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) that arises is established as the "dharma-patience" (*dharmakṣānti*).
The path of liberation that arises is established as dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).

The uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) that arises based on the contemplation of the suchness (*tathatā*) of the suffering truth of the higher realms is established as subsequent patience (*anvayakṣānti*).
The path of liberation that arises [from that] is established as subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
For what reason is the higher realm established as "category" (*gotra*)?
It is because the higher realm is the category that abandons the defilements to be abandoned and realizes the principles to be realized, which were previously severed in the lower desire realm;
thus, the term "category" is applied to the higher realm.
Since it is thus for the Truth of Suffering,
the remaining three truths are to be understood accordingly. Thus,
there are eight paths of uninterrupted realization and eight paths of liberation common to the four truths, which together constitute sixteen [moments].
This refers to the establishment of sixteen moments of mind— divided into categories based on the distinct contemplation of the objects of the truths of the higher and lower realms.

Regarding the "correct abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the three realms," this means that beneath the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) within the three realms, there are twenty-eight types of conceptual afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*).
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are precisely what are severed by the correct wisdom that realizes the true suchness (*tathatā*) of suffering.

Therefore, the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* (receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering) realizes the true suchness of suffering and correctly severs the twenty-eight types of conceptual afflictions belonging to the truth of suffering within the three realms.
Regarding the phrase "among all consciousnesses prior to the seventh stage":
"all consciousnesses" refers to the first seven consciousnesses.
This is because, prior to the seventh stage, they still give rise to the perception of signs (*nimitta*).
The innate obstacles have not yet been fully subdued.
If this is the case for the six consciousnesses,
it is certainly so for the seventh.
Therefore, even before the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) can still arise within the seven consciousnesses.
Regarding the statement "because the inducing consciousness is untainted" (*anāsrava*),
this means that when the first five consciousnesses arise, they must necessarily be induced by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Because it is subtle, inferior, and possesses little discrimination;
because it must rely on the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as its root of discrimination to arise;
and because that consciousness which can induce it is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because the consciousness that is induced does not function due to the absence of obstacles.

Regarding the phrase "when the sixth mental consciousness enters the state of emptiness of beings," it means that the six consciousnesses only arise when the manas-consciousness serves as their specific, non-common basis.
Since that manas-consciousness lacks superior functional capacity,
when one wishes to enter the state of outflowlessness,
it must necessarily be guided by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as its path.
Therefore, when the manovijñāna enters into the emptiness of persons,
the ego-grasping of the manas does not function;
when it enters into the emptiness of phenomena, the grasping at phenomena does not function.
Only then is the wisdom of equality (samatājñāna) fully realized.
Because the seventh consciousness is still characterized by outflows (sāsrava) when the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) enters into the realization of the emptiness of persons (pudgalanairātmya).
The cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) can also arise therein.
Regarding the statement that the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) does not obstruct the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth:
this means that the ten stages are established based on the distinctions of the wisdom of true suchness (*tathatā*) which is empty of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Only the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) can obstruct the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
As for the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it merely incites karma and brings about birth and death;
it obstructs only nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it cannot obstruct the ten stages (*bhūmi*). If that were so,
it would have to be distinct from the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which would contradict the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) doctrine.
Therefore, that text states:
"Among the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), this hindrance must necessarily exist,
for the former definitely takes the latter as its basis."
That treatise further states:
"At the stage when the view of a personal self (*pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) arises,
the view of a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) must also necessarily manifest."
Just as one who is deluded by error might mistake a tree stump for a person,
since it is admitted that the two obstacles and the two attachments are identical in essence,
how can there be a difference in that which is obstructed?
